name: Liquid cooling (direct-to-chip)
thesis: Above ~30–50 kW per rack, air cooling fails — so next-gen GPUs make liquid cooling mandatory, not optional. This is a fast transition more than a hard shortage.

gauge.rationale: Demand is surging as Blackwell-class racks force liquid cooling, but a broad supplier base keeps this a scaling transition rather than a sold-out chokepoint.

why_it_gates: Next-gen accelerators run too hot for air — an H200 dissipates ~700W, and Blackwell-class racks push past what air can economically remove. Without liquid cooling, operators simply can't run high-density racks, so it caps how much compute fits per site. Unlike the silicon and power chokepoints, the constraint here is integration and skilled deployment, not a single-supplier monopoly.

catalysts.text: Blackwell / Rubin-class rollouts make liquid cooling the default, not the exception
Two-phase immersion scales as operators chase higher thermal efficiency
Retrofit of brownfield air-cooled facilities to direct-to-chip

what_loosens_it: Many credible suppliers and fast capacity additions mean supply largely keeps pace with demand; the real constraint is integration and skilled labor rather than a monopoly — which is why this reads tight rather than critical.

developments.text: Data-center liquid cooling market seen ~$6.6B in 2026, scaling to ~$38B by 2033 (28.7% CAGR)
H200's ~700W loads make air cooling uneconomic; direct-to-chip becomes a core architectural requirement
